sections.title: Public Administration: Meaning, Nature and Scope

blocks.text: Public Administration is the organisation and management of public affairs and the implementation of government policies. Its nature is public, service-oriented and closely connected with law and politics. Its scope includes organisation, personnel, finance, policy implementation, development and public service delivery.

Definitions: Woodrow Wilson - 'detailed and systematic execution of public law; every particular application of general law is an act of administration'; L. D. White - 'all those operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'; Luther Gulick - 'that part of the science of administration which has to do with government, and thus concerns itself primarily with the executive branch'; Pfiffner - 'the coordination of individual and group efforts to carry out public policy'; Dwight Waldo - 'the art and science of management as applied to the affairs of state'; and Nigro and Nigro - 'cooperative group effort in a public setting'.

Nature: there are two views - the integral view (L. D. White, Marshall Dimock), which includes all activities, manual, clerical and managerial, in carrying out public policy; and the managerial view (Simon, Smithburg, Thompson, Gulick), which includes only the managerial activities of those at the top who plan, organise, direct and control. Scope: the POSDCORB view (Gulick, 1937 - Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting); the subject-matter view (functions such as defence, education, health, agriculture); and the modern view, which includes policy-making and implementation, organisation, personnel, financial administration, administrative law, comparative and development administration, local government, and public service delivery and governance. Whether Public Administration is an art or a science is debated: it has systematic knowledge and principles, but administration also requires skill, judgement and experience.

Public Administration developed as a separate field of study with the growth of modern government. Early study emphasized organisation, principles and efficiency. Later approaches gave greater attention to human behaviour, comparison, social justice, management, governance and citizen-centred administration.

Nicholas Henry ('Public Administration and Public Affairs') identified five paradigms: (1) the politics-administration dichotomy (1900-1926) - Woodrow Wilson's 'The Study of Administration' (1887), Frank Goodnow's 'Politics and Administration' (1900) and L. D. White's 'Introduction to the Study of Public Administration' (1926), the first textbook; (2) principles of administration (1927-1937) - W. F. Willoughby's 'Principles of Public Administration' (1927), Mary Parker Follett, Henri Fayol, Gulick and Urwick's 'Papers on the Science of Administration' (1937, POSDCORB); (3) challenge and response (1938-1950) - Chester Barnard's 'The Functions of the Executive' (1938), Herbert Simon's 'Administrative Behaviour' (1947) and Robert Dahl, who rejected the dichotomy and the 'principles' as 'proverbs'; (4) Public Administration as Political Science (1950-1970) and Public Administration as Management (1956-1970); and (5) Public Administration as Public Administration (from 1970), with focus on public policy and public affairs.

Later developments include the comparative administration movement (Fred Riggs, Ferrel Heady), development administration (Edward Weidner), New Public Administration (Minnowbrook I, 1968), public choice theory (Vincent Ostrom), New Public Management (1980s-1990s), New Public Service (Denhardt, 2000), governance and network governance, digital-era governance and public value (Mark Moore, 1995). In India, the Indian Institute of Public Administration (1954) promotes the discipline.

Public Administration turns laws and policies into practical action. It maintains public services, supports development and welfare, implements government programmes and helps maintain continuity in government.

Significance: (1) it is the instrument through which government policies and laws are carried out - 'the government in action'; (2) it provides essential services - education, health, water, roads, electricity, transport, sanitation, social security; (3) it maintains law and order, protects life and property, and ensures internal security; (4) it promotes economic development and planning; (5) it implements welfare programmes for the poor, women, children, SCs, STs and other vulnerable groups; (6) it manages disasters and emergencies, such as floods, earthquakes and pandemics (COVID-19 vaccination drives); (7) it collects revenue and manages public finances; (8) it provides continuity and stability when governments change; (9) it acts as an instrument of social change (abolition of untouchability, empowerment of women); and (10) it protects the environment and regulates economic activities.

Brooks Adams said administration is 'the capacity of coordinating many and often conflicting social energies in a single organism'. Charles Beard said, 'There is no subject more important than administration; the future of civilised government and even civilisation itself rests upon our ability to develop a science and a philosophy of administration competent to discharge the functions of civilised society.' In India's welfare state, administration is central to programmes such as MGNREGA, PDS, Jan Dhan, Ayushman Bharat and Swachh Bharat.

Public administration serves public purposes and works under constitutional, legal and political accountability. Private administration mainly serves the objectives of private organisations. Both require planning, organisation, staffing, coordination and management.

Similarities: both involve POSDCORB functions; use similar management techniques (planning, budgeting, human resource management, information technology); require skilled personnel; and deal with organisation and coordination. Henri Fayol, Mary Parker Follett and Lyndall Urwick believed that administration is a universal process, the same in public and private sectors.

Differences (Paul Appleby, Herbert Simon, Josiah Stamp): (1) aim - public administration serves the public interest and welfare, while private administration aims at profit; (2) political character - public administration is subject to political direction and control; (3) accountability - public administration is accountable to the legislature, courts, media and citizens; private administration to owners and shareholders; (4) legal framework - public administration follows laws, rules and procedures (rigid), while private administration is more flexible; (5) consistency of treatment - public administration must treat all citizens equally (principle of uniformity); (6) monopoly - many public services have no competitor; (7) scale and complexity - public administration is much larger and broader; (8) financial control - public funds are controlled by the legislature and audited by the CAG; and (9) public scrutiny - public administration operates in a 'goldfish bowl'. Appleby said 'government is different' because of its breadth of scope, public accountability and political character. In recent decades, New Public Management has reduced some differences through public-private partnerships and business methods in government.
The traditional approach emphasizes formal structures, rules, hierarchy, principles and legal authority. It studies administration mainly through institutions and prescribed arrangements.

The traditional (classical or structural) approach dominated the early twentieth century. It focused on formal organisation, structure, legal authority, rules and procedures, and sought universal 'principles of administration' to achieve efficiency and economy. Thinkers include Woodrow Wilson, Frank Goodnow, L. D. White, W. F. Willoughby, Henri Fayol, Luther Gulick, Lyndall Urwick, James Mooney and Alan Reiley ('Onward Industry', 1931), and Max Weber's bureaucratic model.

Principles include hierarchy, unity of command, span of control, division of work, specialisation, delegation, coordination, centralisation and decentralisation, and line and staff. The approach also includes the legal approach (studying administration through constitutions, laws and court decisions) and the institutional approach. Criticisms: it is static, ignores human behaviour, informal relations and the environment; the 'principles' are not scientific and often contradict each other (Simon called them 'proverbs'); and it focuses on Western contexts.
The historical approach studies administrative institutions through their origin and development over time. It helps explain how present administrative systems evolved.

The historical approach studies the origin, growth and development of administrative institutions over time to understand present structures. For example, Indian administration can be understood through its historical roots: Kautilya's Mauryan administration, the Mughal system (mansabdari, revenue administration of Sher Shah and Todar Mal, divisions into subas, sarkars and parganas), and British colonial administration (the Indian Civil Service, district administration with the Collector, the secretariat system, and the police system established by the Police Act, 1861).

Important works using this approach include those of Jadunath Sarkar ('Mughal Administration'), L. D. White's administrative histories of the USA ('The Federalists', 'The Jeffersonians', 'The Jacksonians', 'The Republican Era'), and studies of the evolution of the Indian Civil Service (Philip Woodruff's 'The Men Who Ruled India'). Merits: it explains continuity and change and the influence of traditions. Limitations: it may be descriptive and may not offer general theories or solutions to current problems.
The philosophical approach examines the values, purposes and principles underlying administration, including ideas about authority, justice and the proper role of the State.

The philosophical (normative) approach is the oldest approach, examining the values, ideals, ethics and purposes of administration. It asks questions such as: What should be the goals of administration? What is the relationship between the state and citizens? What values should guide administrators - efficiency, justice, equity, accountability, responsiveness? Sources include Plato's 'Republic' (rulers as guardians), Aristotle, Confucius, Kautilya, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and the Gita's ideal of selfless action (nishkama karma).

In modern Public Administration, the philosophical approach is represented by Dwight Waldo ('The Administrative State', 1948), who argued that administration is inherently political and value-laden; the New Public Administration movement (emphasis on social equity); John Rawls's theory of justice applied to administration (H. George Frederickson); and debates on administrative ethics, public interest and good governance. Merits: it gives administration a moral direction. Limitations: it may be abstract and subjective.
The behavioural approach studies the actual behaviour of individuals and groups in organisations. It emphasizes observation, motivation, decision-making and human relations.

The behavioural approach developed in the 1940s-1950s, influenced by the human relations school (Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies, 1924-1932) and the behavioural revolution in social sciences. Herbert Simon's 'Administrative Behaviour' (1947) is the classic work; others include Chester Barnard, Chris Argyris, Rensis Likert, Abraham Maslow, Douglas McGregor and Frederick Herzberg.

Features: it studies actual behaviour of individuals and groups in organisations rather than formal structures; it is empirical and uses scientific methods (observation, surveys, experiments, statistical analysis); it is interdisciplinary, drawing on psychology, sociology and anthropology; it emphasises decision-making, motivation, leadership, communication, morale, informal groups and organisational behaviour; and it tries to be value-free. Simon's concepts include bounded rationality, 'satisficing' and the 'administrative man'. Criticisms: excessive focus on methodology and quantification, neglect of values, and limited practical relevance - leading to the post-behavioural emphasis on relevance (New Public Administration).
The comparative approach studies administrative systems across countries and environments in order to identify similarities, differences and the influence of social and political settings.

The comparative approach developed after the Second World War, when Western scholars studied administrative systems in newly independent countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, often supported by US aid programmes. The Comparative Administration Group (CAG, 1960, of the American Society for Public Administration, chaired by Fred Riggs and funded by the Ford Foundation) promoted it. Thinkers include Fred Riggs ('The Ecology of Public Administration', 1961; 'Administration in Developing Countries: The Theory of Prismatic Society', 1964), Ferrel Heady ('Public Administration: A Comparative Perspective', 1966) and Robert Dahl, who argued in 1947 that a science of administration requires comparative study.

It studies the ecology of administration - how social, economic, political and cultural environments influence administrative systems. Approaches include the bureaucratic approach (comparing bureaucracies), the general systems approach (Riggs's models of fused, prismatic and diffracted societies) and the middle-range approach. Merits: it helps develop general theories, learn from other countries and understand the impact of environment. Criticisms: Western bias, abstract models, lack of practical results, and the decline of the CAG in the 1970s.

New Public Administration emphasized social equity, relevance, change and responsiveness. It argued that administration should not focus only on efficiency but also on fairness and the needs of citizens.

New Public Administration (NPA) emerged from the Minnowbrook Conference (1968), organised by Dwight Waldo at Syracuse University for young scholars, in a period of social turmoil in the USA (civil rights movement, Vietnam War, urban riots, poverty). Key contributions came from H. George Frederickson, Frank Marini ('Toward a New Public Administration', 1971), Todd LaPorte and others. The Honey Report (1967) and Philadelphia Conference (1967) also influenced it.

Themes: (1) relevance - administration must address contemporary social problems; (2) values - rejection of value-free administration; (3) social equity - administration should promote the interests of disadvantaged groups (Frederickson); (4) change - administration should be an agent of change rather than maintaining the status quo; (5) client-orientation and citizen participation; (6) decentralisation and democratic decision-making within organisations; and (7) ethics and responsiveness. Minnowbrook II (1988) and III (2008) continued the discussions. Criticisms: anti-theoretical, anti-positivist, vague, and more a mood or movement than a theory; Robert Golembiewski called it a 'temporary radicalism'.
New Public Management applies selected management ideas such as performance, results, efficiency, competition and customer orientation to public organisations.

New Public Management (NPM) emerged in the 1980s in the UK (Margaret Thatcher's reforms - the Financial Management Initiative, Next Steps agencies, privatisation), New Zealand, Australia and the USA (Ronald Reagan, and Bill Clinton and Al Gore's 'National Performance Review', 1993). Christopher Hood (1991) coined the term. David Osborne and Ted Gaebler's 'Reinventing Government' (1992) proposed 'entrepreneurial government' with ten principles, such as catalytic government ('steering rather than rowing'), community-owned, competitive, mission-driven, results-oriented, customer-driven, enterprising, anticipatory, decentralised and market-oriented.

Features (Hood): hands-on professional management, explicit standards and performance measures, emphasis on output controls and results, disaggregation of units into agencies, competition (contracting out, market testing), private-sector management styles and discipline and economy in resource use. Influenced by public choice theory and managerialism. In India, NPM ideas appeared in disinvestment, public-private partnerships, citizens' charters (1997), e-governance, performance management (the Results-Framework Document, 2009) and outsourcing. Criticisms: treats citizens as customers rather than citizens, neglects equity and accountability, weakens public values and may increase inequality and fragmentation.
New Public Service emphasizes democratic citizenship, public interest, participation and accountability. It views citizens as participants in governance rather than merely customers.

New Public Service (NPS) was proposed by Janet V. Denhardt and Robert B. Denhardt ('The New Public Service: Serving, Not Steering', 2000-2003) as an alternative to both traditional public administration and NPM. It draws on democratic citizenship theory, community and civil society, organisational humanism and postmodern public administration.

Seven principles: (1) serve citizens, not customers; (2) seek the public interest; (3) value citizenship over entrepreneurship; (4) think strategically, act democratically; (5) recognise that accountability is not simple (it involves law, community values, political norms, professional standards and citizen interests); (6) serve rather than steer; and (7) value people, not just productivity. NPS emphasises participation, dialogue, collaboration, shared leadership and public values. In India, participatory governance initiatives such as social audits under MGNREGA, gram sabhas, participatory budgeting experiments, and citizen feedback systems reflect NPS ideas.
Formal organisation is deliberately created with defined authority, rules and responsibilities. Informal organisation develops naturally through personal and social relationships among members.

Formal organisation is the planned structure of positions, roles, authority and responsibility designed to achieve organisational goals, expressed through organisational charts, rules, job descriptions and procedures (Weber, Fayol, Gulick). Features: deliberately created, impersonal, based on rules and hierarchy, stable, with official channels of communication and defined goals.

Informal organisation is the network of personal and social relationships, groups, norms, friendships, communication channels (the 'grapevine') and leadership that develops naturally among members. Its importance was revealed by the Hawthorne studies (Mayo) and Chester Barnard, who said informal organisation is essential for the functioning of formal organisation because it provides communication, cohesion and a sense of personal integrity. Merits of informal organisation: satisfies social needs, improves communication and cooperation, fills gaps in formal rules and supports morale. Demerits: resistance to change, rumours, group conflicts and norms that may restrict productivity. Effective managers use both.
Line agencies directly perform the main functions of an organisation. Staff agencies provide advice, research, planning and specialised assistance to line authorities.

Line agencies are concerned with the primary objectives of the organisation and exercise command authority - for example, ministries and departments (Ministry of Health, Ministry of Railways), government corporations, and field offices delivering services. They make decisions, issue orders and are responsible for implementation. The term comes from the military, where line officers command troops.

Staff agencies advise, assist and support line agencies but do not exercise command authority. Types (Willoughby, White): (1) general staff - advise the chief executive on overall policy (the Prime Minister's Office, Cabinet Secretariat, NITI Aayog in India; the Executive Office of the President in the USA); (2) technical staff - provide specialised expertise (legal advisers, engineers, scientists); and (3) auxiliary agencies - provide common services to all departments (the UPSC for recruitment, the Central Public Works Department for construction, the Directorate General of Supplies and Disposals for purchases, the Ministry of Finance for budgeting). Functions of staff: research, planning, advice, coordination, information and reporting. Line-staff conflicts may arise over authority, credit and expertise; solutions include clear definition of roles and cooperation.
Headquarters formulate policy, coordinate and supervise, while field agencies implement programmes and maintain direct contact with local conditions and citizens.

Headquarters (central office) is the main office of an organisation, located in the capital, where policy is formulated, plans are prepared, budgets made, coordination and supervision exercised. Field agencies (field offices) are the units located in different areas (regions, states, districts, blocks, villages) that implement policies and deliver services directly to people, such as district collectorates, police stations, post offices, health centres and agricultural extension offices. About 90 percent of government employees work in field offices.

Relationship: headquarters must give field offices sufficient authority to adapt to local conditions (decentralisation), while maintaining control and uniformity. Problems include delays caused by referring matters to headquarters, lack of understanding of local conditions at headquarters, and inadequate resources in the field. Methods of headquarters-field relations: the unit system (each department has its own field offices) and the prefectoral system (a single coordinating officer, such as the District Collector in India or the prefect in France, coordinates field activities). The Collector in a district coordinates revenue, law and order, development and elections.

sections.title: Meaning, Nature, Scope, Evolution and Significance of Public Administration

blocks.text:
Public Administration refers to the organised activity through which government policies and public programmes are carried out. It is both a practical activity and an academic field.

Its nature is public and service-oriented. It operates under law and political authority and is expected to remain accountable to citizens. Its scope includes organisation, personnel administration, financial administration, implementation of policy, development activities and delivery of public services.

The discipline gradually moved from a strong emphasis on formal organisation and efficiency toward the study of human behaviour, comparative administration, social equity, public management and citizen-centred governance. Its significance has increased because modern governments perform extensive welfare, developmental, regulatory and service functions.

Meaning and nature: Public Administration is the organisation and management of public affairs and the implementation of public policy (Wilson, White, Gulick, Waldo). It has two meanings - an activity (the work of government) and a discipline (the study of that activity). Integral and managerial views; public, service-oriented, law-bound, politically directed and accountable nature. Art and science: it uses systematic knowledge but also requires practical skill. Scope: POSDCORB, subject-matter view and modern scope including policy, organisation, personnel, finance, law, comparative and development administration, local government and governance.

Evolution: Wilson's essay (1887) and the politics-administration dichotomy; principles of administration (1927-1937, Willoughby, Fayol, Gulick and Urwick); challenge (Barnard, Simon, Dahl); public administration as political science and as management; the comparative and development administration movements; New Public Administration (1968); public choice; New Public Management (1980s-1990s); New Public Service; governance, e-governance and public value. The discipline evolved from emphasis on efficiency and structure to concern for behaviour, values, equity, results and citizen participation.

Significance: implements laws and policies, delivers services, maintains order, promotes development and welfare, manages crises, collects revenue, provides continuity and acts as an instrument of social change. In developing countries like India, administration is central to nation-building and development. Public and private administration share managerial techniques, but public administration is distinct in its public purpose, political character, legal framework, accountability and scale (Appleby: 'government is different').

The traditional approach emphasizes formal organisation, rules, hierarchy and established administrative principles. The historical approach explains institutions through their development over time, while the philosophical approach examines the values and purposes behind administration.

Modern approaches broadened the field. The behavioural approach focuses on actual human behaviour, motivation and decision-making within organisations. The comparative approach studies administrative systems across different countries and social environments.

Together these approaches show that administration can be studied from structural, historical, value-based, behavioural and comparative viewpoints.

Traditional approaches: (1) structural or classical approach - formal organisation, principles (hierarchy, unity of command, span of control, specialisation), efficiency (Fayol, Gulick, Urwick, Mooney and Reiley, Weber); (2) legal approach - administration studied through constitutions, laws, rules and court decisions; (3) historical approach - origins and development of institutions (Kautilya, Mughal and British administration in India); and (4) philosophical approach - values, ethics and purposes of administration (Plato to Waldo and NPA).

Modern approaches: (1) behavioural approach - actual human behaviour, decision-making, motivation, leadership, informal groups (Mayo, Barnard, Simon, Maslow, McGregor); (2) comparative approach - study of administration across countries and environments (Riggs, Heady, CAG); (3) ecological approach - interaction between administration and its environment (John Gaus, Riggs); (4) systems approach - administration as a system interacting with its environment (Easton, Katz and Kahn); (5) public choice approach (Vincent Ostrom, applying economics to administration); and (6) management approaches (NPM).

Evaluation: each approach captures a different dimension - structure, law, history, values, behaviour or environment. No single approach is sufficient; a combination gives a fuller understanding. For example, studying Indian district administration requires historical (colonial origins), structural (hierarchy of offices), legal (laws and rules), behavioural (officials' attitudes and decisions) and comparative (lessons from other countries) perspectives.

sections.title: New Public Administration, New Public Management and New Public Service

blocks.text:
New Public Administration emphasized relevance, social equity, change and responsiveness. It argued that administration must consider fairness and the needs of disadvantaged groups in addition to efficiency.

New Public Management introduced a stronger focus on performance, results, efficiency and management techniques. It encouraged public organisations to pay greater attention to outcomes and service quality.

New Public Service places democratic citizenship and public interest at the centre. It emphasizes participation, accountability and serving citizens rather than treating government simply as a business.

New Public Administration (1968, Minnowbrook): a reaction to the value-free behavioural approach and the social crises of the 1960s in the USA; emphasises relevance, values, social equity, change, client-orientation, participation, decentralisation and ethics. It shifted the focus from efficiency to equity and from administration as a neutral tool to administration as an active agent of social justice. Criticisms: vague, anti-theoretical, idealistic, and lacking practical methods.

New Public Management (1980s-1990s): influenced by public choice theory, managerialism and fiscal crises; emphasises efficiency, performance measurement, results, competition, contracting out, privatisation, decentralised agencies and customer orientation ('Reinventing Government', Osborne and Gaebler; 'steering not rowing'); applied in the UK, New Zealand, Australia, the USA and later in India (citizens' charters, PPPs, disinvestment, e-governance). Criticisms: citizens are reduced to customers; equity and democratic accountability are neglected; fragmentation and loss of public values.

New Public Service (2000, Denhardt and Denhardt): serving citizens rather than customers, seeking the public interest, valuing citizenship and democracy, sharing leadership, accepting complex accountability and valuing people. It combines NPA's concern for democracy and equity with a practical focus on participation. These three represent a movement from equity (NPA) to efficiency (NPM) to democratic citizenship (NPS); contemporary governance tries to balance all three values.

Formal organisations are deliberately created with defined rules, authority and responsibilities. Informal organisations arise naturally from personal and social relationships and can influence communication and cooperation.

Line agencies directly carry out the main purposes of an organisation, while staff agencies provide specialised advice and assistance. Headquarters usually formulate policy, coordinate and supervise, whereas field agencies carry out programmes closer to citizens and local conditions.

These arrangements help divide work and connect policy-making with implementation.

Formal and informal organisation: formal organisation is the deliberate structure of positions, authority and rules (charts, job descriptions); informal organisation is the natural network of social relationships, groups and communication (grapevine) revealed by the Hawthorne studies and Barnard. Both are interdependent: formal structure provides order, while informal relations provide cooperation, communication and morale; managers must use informal groups constructively.

Line and staff agencies: line agencies perform primary functions and exercise command (ministries, departments, corporations, field offices); staff agencies advise and assist (general staff - PMO, Cabinet Secretariat, NITI Aayog; technical staff - experts; auxiliary agencies - UPSC, CPWD, finance). Staff agencies help line officials with research, planning and coordination but do not give orders. Conflicts can arise, so roles must be clearly defined and cooperation encouraged.

Headquarters and field agencies: headquarters formulate policy, plan, coordinate, budget and supervise; field agencies implement programmes at regional, district and local levels and interact directly with citizens. Their relationship requires a balance between central control and field discretion. Systems include the unit system and the prefectoral system (the District Collector in India). These arrangements divide work and connect policy-making with implementation.

The Preamble states the basic ideals and objectives of the Constitution. It describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic and expresses the goals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

The Preamble was based on Jawaharlal Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946). It declares that the people of India are the source of authority, describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, and states the objectives: Justice (social, economic and political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), Equality (of status and of opportunity) and Fraternity (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation). 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

For Indian administration, the Preamble sets out the goals that administrators must serve - a welfare state, social justice, equality and dignity. Administration is expected to be impartial, secular, accountable to the people and committed to the unity of the nation. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and reflects its basic structure.

Fundamental Rights are constitutionally guaranteed rights intended to protect liberty, equality and dignity. They place important limits on arbitrary State action and are enforceable through constitutional remedies.

Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) are: the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). They are justiciable and can be enforced through writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto) issued by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226).

Significance for administration: Article 12 defines the 'State' to include the government, Parliament, legislatures and all local and other authorities, so all administrative actions must respect Fundamental Rights. Administrative decisions can be challenged if they are arbitrary, discriminatory or violate rights; courts have developed principles of natural justice (the right to be heard - audi alteram partem; no one should be a judge in their own cause - nemo judex in causa sua), reasonableness and proportionality. Article 14 has been interpreted to prohibit arbitrariness in administration (E. P. Royappa, 1974; Maneka Gandhi, 1978). Article 16 ensures equality of opportunity in public employment and allows reservations.
Directive Principles guide the State in establishing social and economic justice and welfare. They are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental principles for governance.

Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are guidelines for the state to establish a welfare state and social and economic democracy. They include socialist principles (Article 38 - social order based on justice; Article 39 - livelihood, distribution of resources, equal pay; Article 41 - right to work, education, public assistance; Article 42 - just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 43 - living wage), Gandhian principles (Article 40 - village panchayats; Article 43 - cottage industries; Article 46 - educational and economic interests of weaker sections; Article 47 - nutrition, public health, prohibition; Article 48 - agriculture and animal husbandry) and liberal-intellectual principles (Article 44 - Uniform Civil Code; Article 45 - early childhood care and education; Article 48A - environment; Article 50 - separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 - international peace).

Significance for administration: DPSPs guide policy-making and programmes - land reforms, rural development, panchayati raj (73rd Amendment), employment guarantee, food security, health and education schemes, environmental protection and legal aid. They give administration a developmental and welfare orientation, making it an instrument of social change.
Fundamental Duties state important civic responsibilities of citizens, including respect for the Constitution, national unity, public property and the environment.

Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, and the eleventh duty added by the 86th Amendment (2002), include: abiding by the Constitution and respecting its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and Anthem; cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity; defending the country; promoting harmony and renouncing practices derogatory to women; preserving the composite culture; protecting the environment; developing scientific temper; safeguarding public property and abjuring violence; striving for excellence; and providing education to children aged 6-14.

For administration, Fundamental Duties emphasise citizens' cooperation in governance - protecting public property, maintaining harmony, protecting the environment and supporting education. Public servants as citizens are also bound by these duties. They are non-justiciable but can be enforced through specific laws (such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, and environmental laws).

India follows a parliamentary system in which the executive is drawn from and collectively responsible to the legislature. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers exercise the main political executive authority.

India adopted the British (Westminster) model of parliamentary government at the Union (Articles 74-75) and in the states (Articles 163-164). Features: the President (or Governor) is the nominal executive, and the Prime Minister (or Chief Minister) and Council of Ministers are the real executive; the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (or Legislative Assembly); ministers must be members of the legislature (or become members within six months); the majority party forms the government; the Lok Sabha can be dissolved; and the leadership of the Prime Minister.

Implications for administration: ministers are responsible to Parliament for the work of their departments, and civil servants are responsible to ministers (ministerial responsibility); civil servants are politically neutral and anonymous; Parliament controls administration through questions, debates, committees and financial control. The Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary system because of familiarity with British institutions and because it provides daily and periodic accountability (Ambedkar). Challenges include declining parliamentary control, executive dominance and politicisation of the bureaucracy.
Indian federalism divides powers between the Union and States through the Constitution. It combines federal features with a comparatively strong Union government.

Federal features of India: a written and rigid constitution; division of powers between the Union and states through the Seventh Schedule (Union List, State List and Concurrent List); supremacy of the Constitution; independent judiciary; bicameral Parliament with the Rajya Sabha representing states. Unitary features: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union (Article 248), single citizenship, a single constitution, integrated judiciary, All-India Services, appointment of Governors by the Centre, emergency provisions, Parliament's power to change state boundaries (Article 3), and Union law prevailing over state law in the Concurrent List.

Indian federalism has been described as 'quasi-federal' (K. C. Wheare), 'cooperative federalism' (Granville Austin) and 'federation with a centralising tendency' (Ivor Jennings). Administrative federalism involves the implementation of many central laws and schemes by state administrations, the All-India Services serving both, and institutions such as the Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, NITI Aayog (2015) and the GST Council (2016). The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) held federalism to be a basic feature of the Constitution.

The President is the constitutional head of the Union. Executive actions are formally taken in the President's name, while powers are generally exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

The President (Articles 52-62) is elected indirectly by an electoral college for five years. Executive powers (Article 53): all executive actions of the Union are taken in the President's name; the President appoints the Prime Minister and ministers, the Attorney General, the CAG, the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners, the Chairman and members of the UPSC, Governors, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and members of the Finance Commission; administers Union Territories; and makes rules for the conduct of government business (Article 77).

Other powers: legislative (summoning Parliament, assent to bills, ordinances), financial, judicial (pardons), military (Supreme Commander) and emergency powers. Under Article 74 (as amended by the 42nd and 44th Amendments), the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers, though he or she can return advice once for reconsideration. The President has limited discretion (appointment of the PM in a hung Parliament, dismissal of a ministry that has lost majority, pocket veto). The President's role in administration is largely formal, but provides continuity and symbolises the unity of the nation.
The Prime Minister is the head of government and the central figure in the Union executive. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and coordinates major governmental policies.

The Prime Minister is the head of the Union government and the real executive. Appointed by the President as the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha (Article 75). Functions in administration: forms the Council of Ministers and distributes portfolios; presides over the Cabinet and its committees (such as the Cabinet Committee on Security, Appointments Committee of the Cabinet, Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs); coordinates the work of all ministries; resolves inter-ministerial disputes; acts as the link between the Cabinet and the President (Article 78); leads in Parliament; chairs NITI Aayog, the National Development Council, the Inter-State Council and the National Disaster Management Authority; and plays a central role in foreign policy and national security.

The PM controls key appointments (through the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet), the PMO and the Cabinet Secretariat. The PM's power depends on the party's strength, coalition dynamics and personal style. Scholars speak of the 'prime ministerial' form of government in India, especially under strong leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Narendra Modi.
The Council of Ministers aids and advises the President and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. It is headed by the Prime Minister.

The Council of Ministers (Articles 74-75) consists of Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (with independent charge or attached to Cabinet ministers) and Deputy Ministers. The 91st Amendment (2003) limited its size to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha's total strength. The Cabinet is the inner core of senior ministers that takes major decisions; the full Council of Ministers rarely meets as a body. Cabinet committees handle specific areas.

Principles: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)) - all ministers are bound by Cabinet decisions and the ministry must resign if it loses a vote of confidence; individual responsibility - ministers hold office during the President's pleasure (in practice, the PM's) and are responsible for their departments; secrecy. In administration, ministers provide political direction to departments, formulate policies, defend them in Parliament and are accountable for administrative actions, while secretaries and civil servants implement them.
The Central Secretariat assists ministers in policy formulation, coordination, parliamentary work and administrative supervision through ministries and departments.

The Central Secretariat consists of the ministries and departments of the Government of India, located mainly in North Block and South Block (and other buildings, including the new Kartavya Bhavan complex being developed under the Central Vista project) in New Delhi. It is governed by the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, and the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, made under Article 77. There are about 54 ministries and over 90 departments.

Structure of a department (hierarchy): Secretary (administrative head and principal adviser to the minister), Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary (heads a wing), Director or Deputy Secretary (heads a division), Under Secretary (heads a branch), Section Officer (heads a section) and Assistants and clerks. The Secretariat is staffed by officers on tenure deputation from the All-India and Central Services (the 'tenure system', from Lord Curzon's era) and the Central Secretariat Service. Functions: assisting ministers in policy-making; preparing legislation, rules and regulations; budget preparation; coordination with states and other ministries; planning and programme formulation; parliamentary work (answering questions, preparing briefs); supervising attached and subordinate offices; and international relations. Criticisms include delays, excessive hierarchy, file-pushing ('red tape') and generalist dominance.
The PMO provides administrative and advisory support to the Prime Minister and assists in coordination, monitoring and handling matters requiring the Prime Minister's attention.

The Prime Minister's Secretariat was created in 1947 (as a small secretariat under Nehru) and became powerful under Indira Gandhi with P. N. Haksar as principal secretary (1967-1973); it was renamed the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) in 1977 under Morarji Desai. It is a department of the Government of India, headed by the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister and staffed by officers from the civil services and experts. The National Security Adviser also works closely with the PMO.

Functions: assisting the PM in discharging responsibilities as head of government; coordinating with ministries, the Cabinet Secretariat and state governments; monitoring the implementation of major programmes (the PRAGATI platform, 2015, for reviewing projects and grievances); handling the PM's correspondence and public grievances; preparing the PM's speeches and briefs; dealing with matters relating to the PM's relations with the President, Parliament, ministers and foreign dignitaries; and overseeing departments directly under the PM (such as the Department of Atomic Energy and the Department of Space). Critics argue that a powerful PMO centralises power and bypasses the Cabinet and ministries, while supporters say it is necessary for coordination and effective governance.
The Governor is the constitutional head of a State and generally acts on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers, subject to constitutional provisions.

The Governor (Articles 153-162) is appointed by the President for five years, but holds office during the President's pleasure (in practice, the Union government's). Qualifications: citizen of India and at least 35 years old. The same person can be Governor of two or more states (7th Amendment, 1956). Powers: executive (appointing the Chief Minister and ministers, the Advocate General, the State Election Commissioner, members of the State Public Service Commission and vice-chancellors of state universities in many states), legislative (summoning and proroguing the legislature, assent to bills, reserving bills for the President, ordinances under Article 213), financial and judicial (pardons under Article 161).

The Governor acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 163), except in matters where the Constitution requires discretion - such as reserving bills for the President, recommending President's Rule (Article 356), appointing the Chief Minister when no party has a majority, and special responsibilities in certain states (for example, Article 371A for Nagaland, Article 371H for Arunachal; under the Sixth Schedule, the Governor has special powers regarding autonomous district councils, including in Mizoram). The Governor also acts as the agent of the Centre. Controversies include partisan use of the office, delays in assenting to bills (the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor, 2025, set time limits), and the role in government formation. The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended appointing non-partisan persons in consultation with the Chief Minister.
The Chief Minister is the real political executive at the State level, heads the Council of Ministers and plays the central role in State administration.

The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor (Article 164) as the leader of the majority in the Legislative Assembly. Functions: forms the Council of Ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over Cabinet meetings; coordinates the work of departments; is the principal channel of communication between the Governor and the Council of Ministers (Article 167); leads the government in the Assembly; advises the Governor on appointments and dissolution; represents the state in inter-state and Centre-state forums (the Inter-State Council, NITI Aayog Governing Council, Zonal Councils, GST Council); and is the chief spokesperson and political leader of the state.

The Chief Minister controls the state administration through the Chief Secretary and the bureaucracy, and is responsible for law and order, development and welfare programmes. The CM's position depends on the party's majority, coalition partners and the relationship with the central government. In Mizoram, Chief Ministers include Laldenga, Lal Thanhawla, Zoramthanga and Lalduhoma (from December 2023).
The State Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor and is collectively responsible to the State Legislative Assembly.

The State Council of Ministers (Articles 163-164) aids and advises the Governor. It includes Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers. The 91st Amendment (2003) limited its size to 15 percent of the Assembly's strength, but not less than 12 (so small states like Mizoram, with a 40-member Assembly, can have up to 12 ministers). Ministers must be members of the legislature or become members within six months.

The Council is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Article 164(2)), and each minister heads one or more departments. Ministers formulate policy, give direction to departments and are answerable in the Assembly. The relationship between ministers and civil servants follows the same principles as at the Union level: political direction by ministers and implementation by permanent officials.
The State Secretariat assists ministers in policy and coordination. Directorates are generally specialised executive agencies concerned with implementation and technical administration.

The State Secretariat is the central office of the state government, located in the state capital (for example, the Mizoram Secretariat in Aizawl), consisting of departments headed by ministers, with a Secretary (often an IAS officer) as the administrative head of each department. Hierarchy: Chief Secretary, Additional Chief Secretaries or Principal Secretaries, Secretaries, Joint Secretaries, Deputy Secretaries, Under Secretaries and Section Officers. Functions: policy formulation, legislation, budget, planning, coordination, control over executive agencies, relations with the Centre and other states.

Directorates (executive departments) are headed by Directors (often technical experts or senior officers) - such as the Directorate of School Education, Directorate of Health Services, Directorate of Agriculture, Public Works Department (Chief Engineer) - which implement policies and supervise district and field offices. The secretariat is the 'thinking' and policy-making body, while directorates are the 'executing' bodies. Relations between secretariat and directorates may involve duplication, delays and conflicts between generalists (secretaries) and specialists (directors); some states have merged them to improve efficiency.
The Chief Secretary is the senior-most civil servant in the State administration and plays an important coordinating role among departments.

The Chief Secretary is the head of the state's civil service and the senior-most IAS officer in the state, appointed by the Chief Minister (formally by the state government) on the basis of seniority and merit. The post was created during British rule (1799 in Bengal). The Chief Secretary is the secretary to the state Cabinet and the chief adviser to the Chief Minister on administrative matters.

Functions: coordinating all departments of the state government; heading the Cabinet secretariat (preparing agendas and minutes of Cabinet meetings); advising the Chief Minister on policy and administration; supervising the civil service (postings, transfers and discipline of senior officers); chairing important committees (such as on development, coordination and personnel); handling Centre-state relations and communication with the Union Cabinet Secretary; serving as the chief public relations officer of the government; and managing crises, law and order and natural disasters. During President's Rule, the Chief Secretary becomes the principal adviser to the Governor. The Chief Secretary is the counterpart of the Cabinet Secretary at the Union level.
Legislative relations concern the constitutional distribution of law-making powers between Parliament and State Legislatures.

Articles 245-255 and the Seventh Schedule govern legislative relations. Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India (including extra-territorial operation); state legislatures for their state. The Union List (98 subjects - defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways, currency, atomic energy), the State List (59 subjects - police, public order, public health, agriculture, local government) and the Concurrent List (52 subjects - criminal law, marriage, education, forests, trade unions, economic and social planning). Residuary powers belong to Parliament (Article 248). In case of conflict in the Concurrent List, Union law prevails (Article 254), unless the state law received the President's assent.

Parliament can legislate on State List subjects: when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority in the national interest (Article 249); during a national emergency (Article 250); when two or more states request (Article 252); to implement international treaties (Article 253); and during President's Rule (Article 356). Governors can reserve state bills for the President's consideration (Article 200), and some state bills require prior presidential sanction (Article 304). These provisions show the dominance of the Union in legislative relations.
Administrative relations concern the implementation of laws, coordination and constitutional arrangements connecting Union and State executives.

Articles 256-263: states must exercise their executive power to ensure compliance with Union laws (Article 256); the Union can give directions to states on matters such as maintenance of communications of national importance and protection of railways (Article 257); the President can entrust Union functions to states (Article 258) and Governors can entrust state functions to the Union (Article 258A); the Union can adjudicate inter-state water disputes (Article 262, the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956); and the President can establish an Inter-State Council (Article 263; set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation).

Other instruments: All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS, Article 312), whose officers are recruited by the Union but serve in states; the Governor's role; emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360); central armed police forces deployed in states; centrally sponsored schemes implemented by states; Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act, 1956 - the North Eastern Council was created separately in 1971); and NITI Aayog. Issues: misuse of Article 356 (limited by the Bommai judgement), deployment of central forces without state consent, the role of central investigative agencies (CBI requires state consent; several states withdrew general consent), and the use of Governors for political purposes.
Financial relations concern distribution of taxation powers, revenues, grants and other financial resources between the Union and States.

Articles 264-293: the Constitution divides taxing powers - Union taxes (income tax other than agricultural income, corporation tax, customs, central excise on some items, and the Central GST), state taxes (land revenue, agricultural income tax, stamp duties, taxes on alcohol, electricity, vehicles and the State GST) and shared taxes. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) from 1 July 2017, with the GST Council (Article 279A) chaired by the Union Finance Minister and including state finance ministers, an example of cooperative federalism.

The Finance Commission (Article 280), constituted every five years, recommends the distribution of the divisible pool of central taxes between the Union and states (vertical devolution) and among states (horizontal distribution), and grants-in-aid (Article 275). The Fifteenth Finance Commission (N. K. Singh) recommended 41 percent of the divisible pool to states for 2021-2026; the Sixteenth Finance Commission (Arvind Panagariya) covers 2026-2031. Discretionary grants (Article 282), centrally sponsored schemes and borrowing (Article 293 - states need Union consent to borrow if they owe money to the Union) are other aspects. Issues: vertical fiscal imbalance (states have greater responsibilities but fewer resources), dependence of states on central transfers, cesses and surcharges not shared with states, and GST compensation disputes. Mizoram, as a special category state, depends heavily on central transfers.
Corruption is misuse of public office or entrusted authority for private benefit. It weakens public trust, fairness and administrative effectiveness.

The World Bank defines corruption as 'the abuse of public office for private gain'. Forms: bribery, embezzlement, nepotism, favouritism, extortion, fraud, misuse of discretion, collusion with private interests, 'speed money', kickbacks in contracts and procurement, and political corruption (electoral funding, vote buying). Causes: excessive regulation and discretion, complex procedures and delays, low salaries, lack of transparency and accountability, weak enforcement and slow justice, political interference, social acceptance of corruption, monopoly of public services and the nexus between politicians, bureaucrats and business.

Effects: loss of public revenue and inefficiency, poor quality of public services, increased inequality (the poor suffer most), erosion of trust in government, distortion of policies, discouragement of investment, and undermining of democracy and the rule of law. Rajiv Gandhi famously said in 1985 that only 15 paise of every rupee spent on welfare reached the poor. India ranked 96th out of 180 countries in Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index 2024. Major scandals include the Bofors deal, the 2G spectrum case, the Commonwealth Games and the coal block allocation.
Important measures include transparency, accountability, effective vigilance, audit, legal enforcement, citizen access to information, simplified procedures and ethical public service.

Legal measures: the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (amended 2018, which also made bribe-giving an offence and required prior approval for investigating public servants); the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002; the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016; the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014; and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018. Institutional measures: the Central Vigilance Commission (1964, statutory since 2003), the Central Bureau of Investigation (1963), the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (first Lokpal, Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose, appointed in 2019), state Lokayuktas, vigilance departments, the CAG, and the Enforcement Directorate.

Administrative and other measures: the Right to Information Act, 2005; citizens' charters; e-governance and digitalisation (online services, e-procurement - the Government e-Marketplace, GeM, 2016; direct benefit transfers through Aadhaar and Jan Dhan accounts, which reduced leakages); simplification of procedures and reduction of discretion; social audits; time-bound service delivery laws (the Right to Public Services Acts passed by many states); codes of ethics and conduct rules; transparency in political funding; independent media and civil society (the anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare, 2011); and value education. The Santhanam Committee (1964) and the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (4th report, 'Ethics in Governance', 2007) made detailed recommendations.

Indian administration operates within the framework of the Constitution. The Preamble states the ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity and describes the nature of the Indian Republic.

Fundamental Rights protect important individual freedoms and equality. Directive Principles guide the State toward welfare and social justice, while Fundamental Duties emphasize civic responsibility. India follows parliamentary democracy, in which the political executive is responsible to the legislature.

The Constitution also establishes a federal arrangement dividing powers between the Union and States. These constitutional principles shape the organisation, powers and accountability of Indian administration.

Constitutional framework: the Preamble (sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic; justice, liberty, equality and fraternity) sets the goals of administration; Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) limit administrative action - Article 12 brings all authorities within their scope, Article 14 prohibits arbitrariness, Article 16 ensures equality in public employment, and Articles 32 and 226 provide writs; Directive Principles (Articles 36-51) give administration a welfare and developmental orientation (land reforms, panchayats, health, education, employment, environment); Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) emphasise citizens' responsibilities.

Parliamentary democracy: the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature; ministers are accountable for their departments; civil servants are neutral and anonymous and serve ministers; Parliament controls administration through questions, debates, committees (PAC, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings, Departmentally Related Standing Committees) and the budget. Federalism: division of powers between the Union and states, with strong Union features, All-India Services, Governors and centrally sponsored schemes; cooperative federalism through NITI Aayog, the GST Council and the Inter-State Council.

Other constitutional features affecting administration: the independent judiciary and judicial review; constitutional bodies (UPSC and SPSCs, Election Commission, CAG, Finance Commission, National Commissions for SCs, STs and backward classes); safeguards for civil servants (Article 311); local self-government (73rd and 74th Amendments); and special provisions for states and tribal areas (Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Article 371G for Mizoram). The Constitution thus shapes the structure, powers, values and accountability of Indian administration.

The President is the constitutional head of the Union, while the Prime Minister is the head of government and leads the Council of Ministers. The Council aids and advises the President and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The Central Secretariat supports ministers in policy formulation, coordination, parliamentary work and administrative supervision. The Prime Minister's Office provides direct support to the Prime Minister and assists with coordination and monitoring.

Together these institutions connect political leadership with the permanent administrative machinery of the Union government.

President: constitutional head; all executive actions in the President's name; appoints key officials; acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Prime Minister: real head; leads the Council of Ministers, chairs the Cabinet and its committees, coordinates ministries, links the Cabinet and President, leads Parliament and national policy, chairs NITI Aayog and other bodies. Council of Ministers: Cabinet, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers; collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; limited to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha.

Central Secretariat: ministries and departments (Allocation and Transaction of Business Rules, 1961); hierarchy from Secretary to Section Officer; tenure system of staffing; functions - policy-making, legislation, budget, coordination, parliamentary work and supervision of attached and subordinate offices. The Cabinet Secretariat (headed by the Cabinet Secretary, the senior-most civil servant) services the Cabinet and its committees, coordinates ministries and handles crises. PMO: assists the PM, coordinates and monitors programmes (PRAGATI), handles grievances and correspondence, and oversees certain departments; criticised for centralisation.

Evaluation: these institutions connect political leadership (PM and ministers) with the permanent administration (secretaries and officers). Issues include the dominance of the PMO, delays and red tape in the Secretariat, generalist-specialist conflict, and the need for reforms such as lateral entry, e-office, delayering and performance management (recommended by the Second ARC). Effective Union administration depends on coordination, competence and accountability.

At the State level, the Governor is the constitutional head and the Chief Minister is the principal political executive. The Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor and is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

The State Secretariat assists in policy formulation and coordination, while directorates usually perform specialised executive and implementation functions. The Chief Secretary is the senior-most State civil servant and coordinates the administrative machinery.

This structure broadly parallels the parliamentary executive arrangement at the Union level while functioning within the State's constitutional jurisdiction.

Governor: constitutional head of the state, appointed by the President; acts on the advice of the state Council of Ministers except in discretionary matters; also acts as the Centre's representative; special responsibilities in some states (Sixth Schedule areas, Article 371 provisions). Chief Minister: real head of the state government; leads the Council of Ministers, coordinates departments, communicates with the Governor and represents the state in Centre-state forums. Council of Ministers: collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly; size limited to 15 percent of the Assembly (minimum 12).

State Secretariat: departments headed by ministers and secretaries; policy formulation, legislation, budget, planning and coordination. Directorates: headed by directors or technical heads, implementing programmes and supervising field offices (district and block level). The Chief Secretary: head of the state civil service, secretary to the Cabinet, chief coordinator and principal adviser to the Chief Minister, and the link with the Union Cabinet Secretary. District administration under the Deputy Commissioner (in Mizoram and much of the Northeast) or Collector implements state policies at the local level.

Evaluation: state administration parallels the Union structure but operates within the state's constitutional jurisdiction. Problems include secretariat-directorate duplication, politicisation of transfers and postings, delays, limited finances (especially in small states like Mizoram dependent on central grants) and coordination difficulties. Reforms include e-governance, citizen-centred service delivery, decentralisation and capacity-building.

Centre-State relations have legislative, administrative and financial dimensions. Legislative relations concern the distribution of law-making authority. Administrative relations concern implementation and coordination, while financial relations concern taxation, revenue sharing and grants.

Corruption is misuse of public authority for private benefit. It damages public trust and weakens administration. Remedial measures include transparent procedures, accountability, vigilance, audit, legal action, access to information and stronger ethical standards in public service.

Legislative relations: three lists (Union, State, Concurrent), residuary powers with the Union, Union supremacy in conflicts, and Parliament's power to legislate on state subjects in special circumstances (Articles 249, 250, 252, 253, 356); reservation of state bills by Governors. Administrative relations: states must comply with Union laws; Union directions to states; All-India Services; Governors; Article 356; central forces; Inter-State Council; Zonal Councils; NITI Aayog. Financial relations: division of taxing powers; GST and the GST Council; Finance Commission; grants-in-aid; centrally sponsored schemes; borrowing. Commissions on Centre-state relations include the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), the Rajamannar Committee (1969), the Sarkaria Commission (1983-1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2007-2010), which recommended limited use of Article 356, consultation in appointing Governors and greater fiscal autonomy for states.

Corruption: abuse of public office for private gain; forms - bribery, embezzlement, nepotism, extortion, kickbacks; causes - discretion, complex procedures, low accountability, political interference, weak enforcement; effects - inefficiency, inequality, loss of trust. Remedies: legal (Prevention of Corruption Act 1988/2018, PMLA, Benami Act, Whistle Blowers Act), institutional (CVC, CBI, Lokpal and Lokayuktas, CAG, ED), administrative (RTI 2005, citizens' charters, e-governance, DBT, GeM, social audits, Right to Public Services Acts) and ethical (codes of conduct, value education, transparency in political funding).

Conclusion: effective Centre-state relations require cooperative federalism, mutual trust and respect for states' autonomy, while combating corruption requires political will, strong institutions, transparency and citizen participation. Both are essential for good governance in India.
Public Administration means the organisation and management of government activities for public purposes. Its scope includes implementation, organisation, personnel, finance and public services.

Public Administration is the part of administration concerned with government - the organisation, personnel, practices and procedures essential to the effective performance of civil functions entrusted to the executive branch (Marshall Dimock). Woodrow Wilson (1887) is regarded as its founder. Scope: POSDCORB (Gulick) - Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting; subject matter of administration (police, education, health, agriculture, defence); public policy; and modern areas such as development administration, local government and governance.

Public Administration is both an activity (implementing policies and delivering services) and a discipline (studying that activity). Its nature is public, legal, political, service-oriented and accountable. Its importance has increased with the growth of the welfare state, economic development, technology and globalisation.
The discipline developed from the study of formal administrative organisation toward wider attention to behaviour, management, governance and public responsibility.

Stages of evolution: (1) politics-administration dichotomy (Wilson, Goodnow, White, 1887-1926); (2) principles of administration (Willoughby, Fayol, Gulick and Urwick, 1927-1937); (3) challenge (Barnard, Simon's 'Administrative Behaviour', 1947; Dahl, 1947, who argued that public administration cannot be a science without values, behaviour and comparison); (4) crisis of identity (1950-1970), when it was seen as part of political science or management; (5) emergence as a distinct discipline (after 1970), with focus on public policy; (6) New Public Administration (1968), New Public Management (1980s), New Public Service (2000) and governance.

The discipline has thus moved from studying formal structures and efficiency to examining human behaviour, environment, values, social equity, management techniques, citizen participation and governance networks. In India, it is taught as a separate discipline in many universities, including Mizoram University and colleges in Mizoram.
Public administration works for public purposes under legal and political accountability. Private administration mainly serves organisational or business objectives.

Similarities: both use similar management techniques - planning, organising, staffing, coordinating, budgeting and controlling; both require efficiency and skilled personnel; and Fayol and Urwick considered administration universal. Differences: public administration has a political character, aims at public welfare rather than profit, operates under laws and rules, is accountable to the legislature, courts, media and citizens, must treat all citizens equally, often has monopoly over services, is larger in scale, and is subject to public scrutiny and audit by the CAG.

Paul Appleby stressed that 'government is different' because of its breadth of scope, impact and consideration, public accountability and political character. Josiah Stamp emphasised uniformity, external financial control, ministerial responsibility and the marginal profit principle as distinctions. With New Public Management, public organisations have adopted business methods (performance management, PPPs, customer service), but the core public values of equity, accountability and the rule of law remain distinctive.
Formal organisation is officially created with defined authority and duties. Informal organisation develops naturally through social relationships.

Formal organisation: the official structure created by rules, with defined positions, authority, responsibilities, hierarchy, channels of communication and goals (organisational charts). It is planned, impersonal, stable and based on legal-rational authority (Weber). Informal organisation: the unofficial network of personal relationships, friendships, social groups, informal leaders, norms and communication ('grapevine') that arises spontaneously among members.

The Hawthorne experiments (Mayo, 1924-1932) showed that informal groups influence productivity, morale and behaviour - for example, workers in the bank wiring room set their own output norms. Chester Barnard argued that informal organisation is necessary for the functioning of formal organisation. Both coexist: informal relations can support the formal organisation (improving communication and cooperation) or oppose it (resistance to change, rumours). Wise administrators recognise and use informal organisation positively.
Line agencies perform primary functions, while staff agencies advise and assist line authorities.

Line agencies carry out the primary functions of an organisation and exercise command authority, being directly responsible for achieving goals - for example, the Ministry of Railways operating trains, the Department of Police maintaining law and order, and district and block offices delivering services. Types of line agencies in India include ministries and departments, public corporations (such as Air India before privatisation, LIC, ONGC) and independent regulatory bodies (SEBI, TRAI).

Staff agencies advise and assist line officials without command authority. Types: general staff (PMO, Cabinet Secretariat, NITI Aayog), technical staff (legal, engineering and scientific advisers) and auxiliary agencies (UPSC, CPWD, Ministry of Finance for budgetary support, Department of Personnel and Training). Staff agencies provide information, research, planning, advice, coordination and specialised services. The distinction comes from military organisation. Conflicts between line and staff may arise; clear definitions of roles and mutual respect help.
Headquarters usually formulate and coordinate policy; field agencies implement it in local areas.

Headquarters: the central office of a department or organisation, usually located in the capital, which formulates policies, plans programmes, prepares budgets, issues instructions, coordinates and supervises field units, and handles relations with the legislature and other departments. Field units or offices: located at regional, state, district, sub-division, block and village levels, they implement policies, deliver services and interact directly with citizens - such as district offices, police stations, health centres, schools, post offices and agricultural extension offices.

The relationship between headquarters and field offices involves questions of centralisation versus decentralisation: field officers need enough authority to respond to local conditions, while headquarters ensures uniformity and control. In India's prefectoral system, the District Collector or Deputy Commissioner coordinates field administration in the district. Good communication, delegation, inspection and reporting are essential for an effective headquarters-field relationship.
Hierarchy is the arrangement of positions in successive levels of authority from higher to lower offices.

Hierarchy (scalar principle) arranges positions in a pyramid of superior-subordinate relationships, with authority flowing downward and responsibility and communication flowing upward through proper channels. Mooney and Reiley called it the 'scalar process'; Fayol described the 'scalar chain' and allowed the 'gangplank' for horizontal communication. Examples: the military hierarchy, the civil service (Secretary to Section Officer), and district administration (Deputy Commissioner, Sub-Divisional Officer, Block Development Officer).

Advantages: clear lines of authority and responsibility, unity of command, discipline, coordination, delegation and an orderly flow of communication. Disadvantages: rigidity, delays and red tape, distortion of communication across many levels, discouragement of initiative and concentration of power at the top. Modern organisations use flatter structures, teams and digital communication to reduce these problems.
Span of control refers to the number of subordinates directly supervised by one superior.

Span of control (span of supervision or management) refers to the number of subordinates a supervisor can effectively manage. V. A. Graicunas (1933) showed mathematically that as the number of subordinates increases arithmetically, the number of possible relationships (direct single, direct group and cross relationships) increases geometrically; with 5 subordinates there are 100 relationships, and with 6 there are 222. Classical thinkers suggested limits: Ian Hamilton (3-6), Urwick (no more than 5 or 6 at higher levels whose work interlocks), while at lower levels with routine work the span can be larger (Hamilton suggested 10-15).

Factors affecting the span: the nature of work (routine or complex), the competence of the supervisor and subordinates, the degree of delegation, the availability of staff assistance, communication techniques and technology, the physical location of subordinates, and the stability of the organisation. A narrow span leads to tall organisations with many levels (close supervision but delays and costs), while a wide span leads to flat organisations (less supervision but quicker communication and more autonomy). Simon criticised the principle as a 'proverb' conflicting with the need to reduce levels of hierarchy.
