It was adopted on 26 November 1949.

For administration, the Preamble provides the guiding values: administrators must work for social justice and welfare, treat all citizens equally, respect liberty and dignity, remain secular and impartial, and promote national unity. The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and helps interpret it.
Fundamental Rights protect basic freedoms, equality and dignity and are enforceable under the Constitution.

Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35): Right to Equality (14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). They are enforceable through the Supreme Court and High Courts by writs.

Administrative implications: all government authorities must respect Fundamental Rights (Article 12); administrative action must be fair, reasonable and non-arbitrary (Article 14 - Maneka Gandhi, 1978); natural justice must be followed; public employment must be based on equality of opportunity (Article 16), with reservations for disadvantaged groups; and citizens can challenge administrative decisions through writs. Fundamental Rights thus act as limits on administrative power and protect citizens.
Fundamental Duties describe important responsibilities expected of citizens.

Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 86th Amendment (2002). They include respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem; cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity; defending the nation; promoting harmony and respecting women; preserving the composite culture; protecting the environment; developing scientific temper; safeguarding public property; striving for excellence; and providing education to children aged 6-14.

They remind citizens that rights come with responsibilities and encourage cooperation with the administration, for example in protecting public property, maintaining cleanliness, conserving the environment and supporting education. They are not enforceable by courts directly but can be promoted through laws and awareness.
Directive Principles guide the State in pursuing welfare and social and economic justice.

Directive Principles (Articles 36-51) guide the state to promote welfare - adequate livelihood, equitable distribution of resources, equal pay, the right to work and education, humane working conditions, living wages, village panchayats, cottage industries, welfare of weaker sections, public health, nutrition, agriculture, environment, a uniform civil code, separation of judiciary and executive, and international peace.

Administration implements DPSPs through policies and programmes - land reforms, panchayati raj, MGNREGA, the Right to Education, the National Food Security Act, health missions, environmental laws, legal aid and welfare schemes for SCs, STs, women and children. DPSPs give Indian administration its welfare and developmental character, making it an agent of social and economic change.
The President is the constitutional head of the Union executive.

The President is elected indirectly for five years and is the constitutional head of the Union. All executive actions are taken in the President's name (Article 77). The President appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers, Governors, judges, the CAG, the Chief Election Commissioner, members of the UPSC and the Finance Commission, and ambassadors.

The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74) and has only limited discretion. In administration, the President's role is mostly formal, but it ensures constitutional continuity and acts as a check (for example, returning advice for reconsideration, seeking information from the Prime Minister under Article 78).
The Prime Minister heads the government and leads the Union Council of Ministers.

The Prime Minister is the real executive and the head of government. Appointed by the President as leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister selects ministers, allocates portfolios, presides over the Cabinet, coordinates ministries, communicates decisions to the President, leads Parliament, chairs NITI Aayog and other bodies, and plays a central role in policy-making, appointments and foreign affairs.

The Prime Minister's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat assist the PM in coordination and monitoring. The PM's power depends on the strength of the majority, coalition partners and personal leadership.
The Union Council of Ministers aids and advises the President and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The Union Council of Ministers includes Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers; its size is limited to 15 percent of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003). The Cabinet is the key decision-making body, assisted by Cabinet committees (Security, Economic Affairs, Appointments, Political Affairs, Parliamentary Affairs and others).

Principles: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha - the ministry must resign if it loses majority support; individual responsibility of ministers for their departments; and confidentiality. Ministers provide political direction, while secretaries and civil servants implement policies.
The Central Secretariat assists Union ministers in policy, coordination and administrative work.

The Central Secretariat consists of ministries and departments of the Government of India, organised under the Allocation of Business Rules and Transaction of Business Rules (1961). Each department is headed by a Secretary, with Additional Secretaries, Joint Secretaries, Directors, Deputy Secretaries, Under Secretaries and Section Officers. Officers come mainly through the tenure system (deputation from All-India and central services) and the Central Secretariat Service.

Functions: assisting ministers in policy formulation, drafting legislation, preparing budgets, coordinating with other ministries and states, handling parliamentary work and supervising attached and subordinate offices. Reforms include e-office (digital files), delayering of hierarchy and lateral entry.
The PMO provides administrative and advisory assistance to the Prime Minister.

The PMO, headed by the Principal Secretary to the PM, assists the Prime Minister in policy-making, coordination and monitoring of government programmes, handling correspondence and public grievances, preparing speeches and briefs, and overseeing departments under the PM (Atomic Energy, Space). It became powerful under Indira Gandhi and has remained influential.

The PMO helps ensure coordination and quick decision-making but has been criticised for centralising power and reducing the role of ministers and the Cabinet. The Cabinet Secretariat (headed by the Cabinet Secretary) also coordinates ministries and services the Cabinet.
The Governor is the constitutional head of the State.

The Governor (Articles 153-162) is appointed by the President for five years (holding office during the President's pleasure). The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and ministers, summons the legislature, assents to bills or reserves them for the President, promulgates ordinances, and grants pardons. The Governor acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers except in discretionary matters (such as recommending President's Rule and appointing the CM in a hung assembly).

The Governor is also the link between the Centre and the state. In Mizoram and other Sixth Schedule states, the Governor has special responsibilities regarding Autonomous District Councils. Controversies over the role of Governors include partisan behaviour and delays in assent to bills.
The Chief Minister is the head of the State government and leads the State Council of Ministers.

The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor as the leader of the majority in the Legislative Assembly. The CM forms the Council of Ministers, allocates portfolios, presides over Cabinet meetings, coordinates departments, communicates with the Governor (Article 167), leads the Assembly, and represents the state in national forums.
The CM controls the state administration with the help of the Chief Secretary and is responsible for development, law and order and welfare in the state.
The State Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor and is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

The State Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, aids and advises the Governor (Article 163). It is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Article 164(2)). Its size is limited to 15 percent of the Assembly's strength, with a minimum of 12 ministers.
Ministers head departments, frame policies, defend them in the Assembly and are accountable for administration, while civil servants implement policies. The Cabinet takes major decisions.
The Secretariat supports policy and coordination, while directorates generally perform specialised executive functions.

The State Secretariat in the state capital consists of departments headed by ministers and secretaries; it formulates policies, prepares laws and budgets, coordinates and controls executive agencies. Directorates (such as Health Services, School Education, Agriculture) are headed by directors or technical heads who implement policies through district and field offices.

Coordination between the secretariat (policy) and directorates (execution) is important; duplication and delays are common problems, and some states have merged secretariat and directorate functions to improve efficiency.
The Chief Secretary is the senior-most State civil servant and an important coordinator of State administration.

The Chief Secretary is the head of the state civil service, the senior-most IAS officer in the state, appointed by the state government. The Chief Secretary is secretary to the Cabinet, chief adviser to the Chief Minister, coordinator of all departments, and the link with the Union government (through the Cabinet Secretary).

Functions include coordinating departments, chairing committees, supervising senior officers, managing crises and disasters, and advising on administrative matters. During President's Rule, the Chief Secretary becomes the main adviser to the Governor.
Centre-State relations concern the constitutional division and coordination of legislative, administrative and financial powers between Union and States.

Legislative relations: Union, State and Concurrent Lists; residuary powers with the Union; Union law prevails in conflicts; Parliament can legislate on state subjects in special circumstances. Administrative relations: states must comply with Union laws; Union directions; All-India Services; Governors; Article 356; Inter-State Council; Zonal Councils. Financial relations: division of taxes; GST and the GST Council; Finance Commission; grants-in-aid; centrally sponsored schemes.

Issues: misuse of Article 356, the role of Governors, financial dependence of states, and demands for greater autonomy. Commissions (Sarkaria, Punchhi) recommended greater cooperation and consultation. Cooperative federalism through NITI Aayog and the GST Council aims to improve relations.

Indian administration functions within the Constitution. The Preamble expresses the basic ideals of the Republic. Fundamental Rights protect citizens, Fundamental Duties emphasize civic responsibility and Directive Principles guide the State toward welfare and social justice.

These provisions establish the constitutional values within which administrative institutions must function.

The Constitution is the foundation of Indian administration. The Preamble sets out the goals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Fundamental Rights limit administrative power and protect citizens (Article 12 brings all authorities within their scope; Article 14 prohibits arbitrariness; Article 16 ensures equality in public employment). Directive Principles guide administration towards welfare, social justice and development. Fundamental Duties encourage citizens' responsibilities and cooperation.

Other constitutional provisions shaping administration include parliamentary government (ministerial responsibility), federalism (division of powers and All-India Services), constitutional bodies (UPSC, CAG, Election Commission, Finance Commission), safeguards for civil servants (Articles 310-311), local self-government (73rd and 74th Amendments) and special provisions for states and tribal areas (Article 371G, Sixth Schedule for Mizoram). These provisions establish the values and framework within which administrative institutions function.

The President is the constitutional head, while the Prime Minister leads the government and Council of Ministers. The Council is responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The Central Secretariat assists in policy formulation and coordination, while the Prime Minister's Office supports the Prime Minister in important administrative and policy matters. These institutions together form key parts of central administration.

The President is the constitutional head, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Prime Minister leads the government, chairs the Cabinet, coordinates ministries and represents the nation. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The Central Secretariat (ministries and departments under Secretaries) assists in policy, legislation, budgeting and coordination. The Cabinet Secretariat coordinates the Cabinet and ministries. The PMO supports the Prime Minister in policy-making, coordination and monitoring. Together, these institutions link political leadership with the permanent bureaucracy at the Union level.

The Governor is the constitutional head of the State, while the Chief Minister leads the State government and Council of Ministers. The State Secretariat assists policy and coordination, directorates perform specialised executive functions, and the Chief Secretary is the senior-most coordinating civil servant.

Centre-State relations connect the Union and State governments through the constitutional distribution and coordination of legislative, administrative and financial authority.

State administration: the Governor (constitutional head), the Chief Minister and Council of Ministers (real executive, responsible to the Legislative Assembly), the State Secretariat (policy and coordination), directorates (implementation) and the Chief Secretary (head of the civil service and coordinator). District administration under the Deputy Commissioner or Collector implements policies at the local level.

Centre-state relations: legislative (lists and Union supremacy), administrative (directions, All-India Services, Governors, Article 356) and financial (taxes, GST, Finance Commission, grants). Issues include centralisation, the role of Governors and fiscal dependence; solutions include cooperative federalism, consultation and the recommendations of the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions. Mizoram, as a small special category state, relies heavily on central funding and benefits from cooperative arrangements such as the North Eastern Council and the Ministry of DoNER.
